solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Very small item with no power written by journalist?

indicators.note: with no says a letter is to be dropped from the word before it

parts.note: a particle is a tiny piece of matter
P is the standard abbreviation for power in physics

explanation.surface: A query about a tiny piece of writing, powerless, filed by a reporter.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is cryptic: a piece written by a journalist; 'item' does double duty in the surface only.
explanation.definitionFit: A newspaper piece produced by a reporter is called a story or feature, a usual sense of the word.

clue.text: Check Sartre translation

indicators.note: translation says the letters are rendered into a different form

explanation.surface: Proofreading a French version of the philosopher's work.
explanation.definitionFit: To halt or stop something is to check it, as in checking the spread of a disease.

clue.text: Boy initially stuck in test to do with ethnic groups

indicators.note: stuck in says one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: a trial is a test

indicators.note: initially picks the first letter of the word before it

explanation.surface: A lad trapped in an exam on anthropology.
explanation.definitionFit: Relating to clans or peoples sharing kinship and culture is a direct adjectival sense.

clue.text: Not stopping study can lead to unionists in government

parts.note: to con is an old word meaning to study
a tin is a can
U is short for Unionist in Northern Irish politics

explanation.surface: Research suggesting unionists might end up in power.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lead to' is a link joining the pieces; CON for study is a crossword staple.
explanation.definitionFit: Going on without a pause is a straightforward synonym of not stopping.

clue.text: Consumed neat absinthe finally with a twist

indicators.note: finally picks the last letter of the word before it
with a twist says the letters are twisted into a new order, as a cocktail garnish pun

explanation.surface: A drinker downing undiluted absinthe served with a twist of lemon.
explanation.definitionFit: Food that has been eaten has been consumed, both past participles.

clue.text: Dwellings head of aristocracy might be seen in?

definitions.text: Dwellings head of aristocracy might be seen in?

indicators.note: might be seen in says one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: places can mean homes, as in 'come back to my place'

indicators.note: head of picks the first letter of the word that follows

explanation.surface: A wry question about the kind of grand house where an aristocrat lives.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines: the grand homes where a nobleman might live.
explanation.definitionFit: Stately royal or noble residences are the homes where an aristocratic leader could plausibly be found.

clue.text: One might be seen on the tube

definitions.text: One might be seen on the tube

parts.words: One might be seen on the tube
parts.note: the tube is slang for television, not the London Underground

explanation.surface: Something a commuter spots on the London Underground.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tube is London's Underground railway, but 'the tube' is also slang for television.
explanation.definitionFit: A broadcast show is something viewers watch on television, nicknamed the tube.

clue.text: Twisted lips to speak imperfectly

indicators.note: twisted says the letters are bent into a different order

explanation.surface: Contorting the mouth to talk badly.
explanation.definitionFit: Pronouncing s sounds as th is a speech defect, so the verb means speaking imperfectly.

clue.text: Think carefully about prisoners before dire reforms

parts.note: cons are convicts

indicators.note: reforms says the letters are formed again in a new order

explanation.surface: Weighing up prisoners' prospects ahead of harsh penal changes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'before' is a link word placing the prisoners ahead of the reworked letters in this charade.
explanation.definitionFit: To ponder or weigh something up is to think about it carefully.

clue.text: American writers in south-east creating tension

indicators.note: in says the pieces before it go inside the next one

parts.note: pens are writing instruments

explanation.surface: American authors based in the south-east of England building drama.
explanation.definitionFit: The anxious uncertainty felt while awaiting an outcome is a form of tension.

clue.text: Grin with glee finally breaking rule

indicators.note: breaking says the letters before are smashed apart and rearranged
finally picks the last letter of the word before it

explanation.surface: Someone grinning gleefully as they break a regulation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'breaking' looks like it governs 'rule' but it is the anagram signal for GRIN plus E.
explanation.definitionFit: A monarch's period of sovereignty is the term for ruling, so the noun swaps for rule.

clue.text: M&M hordes?

parts.note: M is the Roman numeral for a large round figure, and a pair of them read as a plural; hordes are vast crowds

explanation.surface: Crowds of fans of a sweet brand or a rapper.
explanation.walkthrough: The letter M stands for 1,000 in Roman numerals, so the doubled letter hints at a plural of that number, while hordes are great crowds.
explanation.definitionFit: Countless crowds are commonly described as numbering in the many multiples of a thousand.

clue.text: Firm's papers read out

indicators.note: read out says the word is spoken, giving a different spelling that sounds alike

parts.note: stationery is writing paper and envelopes

explanation.surface: A company's documents being read aloud at a meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Firm' looks like a business, but it is the adjective meaning not moving; 'read out' signals the homophone.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unmoving and fixed in place can be described as firm, a standard synonym.

clue.text: Regular supporter of Boris Johnson?

parts.note: London's public hire cycles were nicknamed after Boris Johnson, mayor when they launched, so the thing he championed is a two-wheeler

explanation.surface: A question about a loyal backer of the former British prime minister.
explanation.walkthrough: London's hire cycles were nicknamed after Boris Johnson, mayor of London when they were launched; he was also a keen cyclist.
explanation.definitionFit: A pedal cycle regularly carries its rider, punningly supporting the former London mayor.

clue.text: One lengthens rope endlessly twisted on farm vehicle

indicators.note: twisted says the remaining letters are wound into a new order
endlessly says the last letter of the word is cut off

parts.note: a tractor is the standard farm vehicle

explanation.surface: A rope coiled up on a tractor in a farmyard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endlessly' cuts ROPE to ROP and 'twisted' makes PRO; 'on' places it above TRACTOR in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who drags things out or prolongs them is one who lengthens, the literal sense of the word.

clue.text: Shops' excellent brand set to be changed

parts.note: super means excellent
a mark is a brand or stamp

indicators.note: to be changed says the letters of the word before are rearranged

explanation.surface: A retailer's top-quality label getting a makeover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be changed' turns SET into ETS; 'Shops'' with its apostrophe stands for the plural noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Large self-service grocery stores are a kind of shop, so the plural swaps for shops.

clue.text: They fix parties in office

parts.note: polls decide which political group holds power, rather than anyone arranging a celebration

explanation.surface: Someone rigging celebrations at the workplace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fix' suggests rigging and 'parties' office celebrations, but it means votes settle which political party governs.
explanation.definitionFit: Public votes determine which political grouping takes up government, putting parties in office.

clue.text: Party decorations and dance soon arranged

parts.note: a ball is a formal dance

indicators.note: arranged says the letters are put in a new order

explanation.surface: Decorating for a party ahead of a dance soon.
explanation.definitionFit: Inflated rubber bags are a classic decoration hung up at celebrations.

clue.text: Excitedly procure ultimate in bread maker

indicators.note: excitedly says the letters are thrown about into a new order
ultimate in picks the last letter of the word that follows

explanation.surface: Eagerly obtaining the best bread-making machine.
explanation.definitionFit: One who creates or manufactures goods is a maker, a general synonym.

clue.text: Plans to develop great manners

indicators.note: to develop says the letters of the following words grow into a new shape

explanation.surface: Schemes intended to cultivate fine etiquette.
explanation.definitionFit: Plans and preparations made in advance are synonyms, as in making travel provisions.

clue.text: Flicks mince around middle of plate

indicators.note: around says the letters are moved about into a new order
middle of picks the central letter of the word that follows

explanation.surface: Someone flicking minced meat around a dinner plate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flicks' looks like a verb but is old slang for films; 'around' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The flicks is informal British slang for the movies or a picture house.

clue.text: Cold blast?

parts.note: a cold means the illness here, and the blast is the sudden explosive expulsion of air it causes

explanation.surface: A gust of icy wind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cold' suggests chilly weather, but it is the common cold.
explanation.definitionFit: A head cold brings on violent bursts of air from the nose, a fitting description.

clue.text: Female to produce eggs around bottom of shed

indicators.note: around says the first piece encloses the second

parts.note: hens lay eggs

indicators.note: bottom of picks the last letter of the word that follows

explanation.surface: A hen laying eggs around the back of a farm shed.
explanation.definitionFit: A polite word for a woman, used as the noun for a female person.

clue.text: Cost of zero fare?

parts.note: if fare means food rather than a ticket price, having none of it exacts a heavy toll

explanation.surface: A question about the price of a free ticket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fare' looks like a travel price, but here it is food; going without food has a grim cost.
explanation.definitionFit: Going without any food at all leads to extreme hunger, the price paid for an empty plate.

clue.text: Where musicians relax in bars

parts.note: bars are measures of music, and the silent pauses written in them are where players stop

explanation.surface: Band members unwinding in a pub after a gig.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bars' looks like pubs, but it means measures of written music containing silent beats.
explanation.definitionFit: In notation, silent beats in a measure are the places a player takes a break.

clue.text: Some pandas, I assume, can be found here?

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A guess about where pandas can be found.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is also true: giant pandas live in China, so the clue works as a whole.
explanation.definitionFit: Pandas live wild only in China, part of this continent, so it is where they are found.

clue.text: Produces events

definitions.meaning: to occasion something is to cause or bring it about

explanation.definitionFit: The word works as a verb meaning brings about and as a plural noun for particular happenings.

clue.text: He met extraordinary argument

indicators.note: extraordinary says the letters are put into an unusual order

explanation.surface: Someone encountering a remarkable line of reasoning.
explanation.definitionFit: The central subject or thesis of an essay or speech is its main argument.

clue.text: Yells and flees, holding end of purse

indicators.note: holding says the first piece clutches the second inside it

parts.note: scrams is slang for runs away

indicators.note: end of picks the last letter of the word that follows

explanation.surface: A thief shouting and running off while clutching a purse.
explanation.definitionFit: Loud piercing cries are shouts, so the plural noun or verb matches yells.

clue.text: Family label certain to get man drunk inside

indicators.note: inside says one piece goes within the other

parts.note: sure means certain

indicators.note: drunk says the letters of man are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone confident they can get a fellow tipsy at a family gathering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to get' is a link; 'drunk' signals the jumbling of the man, which then sits inside the word for certain.
explanation.definitionFit: The name shared by members of a household, passed down the line, labels the family.
